Duty Description: The UX Design duty is about shaping how a product actually works for the people using it, turning rough ideas into screens and flows that feel simple. Day to day that means sketching wireframes, building clickable prototypes, and pulling patterns together into a design system so the whole product feels like one coherent thing. Designers rarely work in a straight line; they try something, put it in front of people, and refine it as the team learns.
What Does It Take for This Duty To Succe: It takes a mix of craft and people skills: interaction design, information architecture, and prototyping to build the work, plus the openness to share ownership and take feedback without ego. Comfort in tools like Figma and Figjam helps, but the real skill is staying curious about whether a design truly makes sense for a real person.
Why Is This Duty Important to Project Su: Design is where a plan becomes something people can see and touch. This duty owns deliverables like wireframes and prototypes that the rest of the team builds on, and it stays active from early discovery through launch, so the product keeps improving instead of freezing at version one.
You might enjoy this duty if you like turning fuzzy problems into clear, usable designs, enjoy sketching and iterating, and get satisfaction from watching a rough idea become something people find easy to use.
Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

Duty Description: The UX Research duty is the team's link to real users. Instead of guessing what people need, researchers plan and run studies, interviews, usability tests, and surveys, then turn what they hear into clear findings the whole team can act on. It is ongoing work; strong teams keep discovering all the way through a project rather than researching once and moving on.
What Does It Take for This Duty To Succe: Succeeding here takes real research skills like interviewing, experiment design, and spotting patterns in messy data, along with the ability to tell a clear story with what you find. Just as important are the team habits: listening well, staying curious, and building enough trust that people share honest feedback.
Why Is This Duty Important to Project Su: This duty keeps the team honest about what users actually need, so effort goes toward real problems instead of assumptions. Its research plans and reports feed decisions at every milestone, and by surfacing issues early it saves the team from building the wrong thing.
You might enjoy this duty if you are curious about people, like listening more than talking, and get a kick out of turning messy human behavior into clear insight the team can use.
Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

Duty Description: The Business Analysis duty turns fuzzy requests into a clear, shared picture of what to build. Analysts gather requirements, write user stories and acceptance criteria, and shape problem statements so everyone agrees on what needs to happen and how they will know it is done. In agile work they write just enough to get moving and keep refining as the team learns.
What Does It Take for This Duty To Succe: It takes a knack for asking good questions and translating between people, plus skills like requirements management, writing user stories, and defining acceptance criteria. The strongest analysts pair that with patience, active listening, and the facilitation skills to get a room to agree.
Why Is This Duty Important to Project Su: Clear requirements are one of the biggest reasons projects succeed or quietly fail. This duty produces the acceptance criteria and user stories the whole team builds against, so designers and developers stop working from different assumptions and expensive rework never happens.
You might enjoy this duty if you like untangling messy problems, enjoy detail, and are good at translating between what people say they want and what the team can actually build.
Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

Duty Description: The Product Ownership duty decides what the team should build next and in what order. Owners maintain the backlog, prioritize the work, and keep a roadmap so the team always has a clear, ranked list to pull from. Priorities shift as the team learns, so this is constant, iterative work rather than a plan set once at the start.
What Does It Take for This Duty To Succe: It takes sharp prioritization, backlog and epic management, and the judgment to say this now, that later, and explain why. Add strong stakeholder skills, since much of the job is balancing many voices and building buy-in for the plan.
Why Is This Duty Important to Project Su: This duty keeps the team pointed at the most valuable work instead of doing a little of everything. By owning the backlog and sprint goals, it turns a big pile of ideas into a focused plan, which is what lets an agile team ship steadily.
You might enjoy this duty if you like making decisions, can weigh many priorities at once, and enjoy owning the details of getting the right thing delivered.

Duty Description: The Product Management duty sets the direction for a product, the what and the why behind the work. Managers dig into users and the market, shape the vision and strategy, and rally the team around which problems are worth solving. They do not build it all themselves; they help everyone pull in the same direction.
What Does It Take for This Duty To Succe: It takes strategic thinking, market and customer insight, and the storytelling to get people behind a vision. Because a manager works through others, the people skills, influence, negotiation, and clear communication, matter as much as the strategy itself.
Why Is This Duty Important to Project Su: This duty makes sure the team is building something people actually want and the business can sustain. By owning the vision, roadmap, and go-to-market plan, it connects users, business, and technology so the whole project has a clear point.
You might enjoy this duty if you like strategy, enjoy connecting people, business, and technology, and are comfortable making calls with incomplete information.

Duty Description: The Scrum Master duty helps a team run smoothly using agile methods like Scrum. Rather than managing people, scrum masters facilitate the rhythm of the work, sprint planning, retrospectives, and demos, and clear roadblocks so the team can focus. A lot of the job is protecting the process and helping the team keep improving.
What Does It Take for This Duty To Succe: It takes facilitation skills, a solid grasp of Scrum, and the patience to guide without controlling. The best scrum masters are strong listeners and conflict-resolvers who help a team surface problems and fix them together.
Why Is This Duty Important to Project Su: This duty keeps an agile team's engine running. By facilitating sprints and retrospectives, it helps the team deliver in steady cycles and get a little better each time, which is the whole point of working in an agile way.
You might enjoy this duty if you like helping a team work well together, enjoy facilitating over directing, and find satisfaction in removing the obstacles that slow people down.
Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

Duty Description: The Project Management duty keeps the work organized and moving. Project managers track what needs to happen, watch the schedule and risks, and keep clients and teammates in the loop so nothing important slips. Much of the job is communication and clearing roadblocks before they slow the team down.
What Does It Take for This Duty To Succe: It takes organization, clear communication, and the ability to stay calm when a lot is in motion. Skills like project management, meeting facilitation, and stakeholder management help, along with the people sense to keep everyone aligned.
Why Is This Duty Important to Project Su: This duty is the glue that holds a project together. By tracking milestones, managing risk, and keeping the client relationship healthy, it lets the rest of the team focus on the work instead of the logistics.
You might enjoy this duty if you like structure, enjoy helping others do their best work, and stay level-headed when things get busy.
Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

Duty Description: The Development duty builds the product, turning designs and requirements into working software. Developers write and document code, build APIs and databases, and deploy what they make so it runs the way it should. It is problem-solving work, breaking a big challenge into small pieces and getting each one working, often in short cycles alongside the rest of the team.
What Does It Take for This Duty To Succe: It takes solid technical skills, programming, database work, and API design, plus the logical thinking to debug problems methodically. The strongest developers also collaborate well, since building software is a team sport that depends on shared ownership and clear communication.
Why Is This Duty Important to Project Su: This duty is where the product actually gets made. The code, APIs, and databases it produces are the working thing users rely on, so the care put in here shows up directly in whether the product holds together.
You might enjoy this duty if you like logic and building things, enjoy solving technical puzzles, and feel real satisfaction when something you made finally runs.
Where Can I Learn More?: MDN Web Docs, a trusted resource for building software: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Learn

Duty Description: The Solutions Architecture duty designs the technical foundation a product is built on. Architects map out how the system fits together, its databases, services, network, and hosting, so developers have a solid, scalable base to build against. It is big-picture technical work that shapes how well everything else holds up.
What Does It Take for This Duty To Succe: It takes deep systems thinking and strong skills in database and network architecture, plus the ability to weigh trade-offs and explain them clearly. Good architects balance what is ideal with what the team can realistically build and maintain.
Why Is This Duty Important to Project Su: This duty sets the technical direction that everything else depends on. A sound architecture lets the product scale and stay stable, while a shaky one causes problems that surface long after launch, so getting it right early matters.
You might enjoy this duty if you like seeing the whole system at once, enjoy solving structural puzzles, and care about building something that will hold up as it grows.
Where Can I Learn More?: MDN Web Docs, a trusted resource for building software: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Learn

Duty Description: The Information Security Analysis duty protects a product and its users from threats. Analysts model how something could be attacked, test for weaknesses, configure defenses, and audit the system to keep data safe. It is careful, detail-driven work that looks for problems before someone with bad intent does.
What Does It Take for This Duty To Succe: It takes a security mindset, network knowledge, and the patience to probe a system for weak spots. Strong analysts pair technical skill with clear communication, since much of the job is explaining risks in a way the team can act on.
Why Is This Duty Important to Project Su: This duty keeps trust intact. A single security gap can undo a lot of good work and harm the people a product serves, so by finding and closing weaknesses early, this duty protects both users and the team's reputation.
You might enjoy this duty if you like thinking like a puzzle-solver, enjoy finding weak spots others miss, and care about keeping people and their data safe.
Where Can I Learn More?: OWASP, the open community for software security: https://owasp.org/

Duty Description: The UX Writing duty crafts the words inside a product, the buttons, labels, messages, and instructions that guide people along. Writers shape a clear voice, build style guides, and cut anything confusing so the product feels simple to use. It sounds small, but the right words can make or break whether people understand what to do.
What Does It Take for This Duty To Succe: It takes a love of clear language, strong writing and editing skills, and an eye for how words fit into a design. Add empathy and collaboration, since good UX writing comes from understanding users and working closely with designers and researchers.
Why Is This Duty Important to Project Su: This duty is what makes a product feel clear instead of confusing. Its words appear at every step users take, so strong writing quietly guides people through the experience and reduces the friction that makes them give up.
You might enjoy this duty if you love words, care about making things easy to understand, and enjoy finding the simplest way to say something.
Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

Duty Description: The Agile Coaching duty helps teams work better together, not by managing them but by guiding how they collaborate. Coaches teach agile ways of working, run workshops, and help a team build trust, ownership, and steady improvement. Much of the job is noticing how people interact and gently helping them get unstuck.
What Does It Take for This Duty To Succe: It takes strong coaching and facilitation skills, deep familiarity with agile methods, and the patience to guide rather than direct. The best coaches lead with empathy and read a team's dynamics well enough to know when to step in and when to hold back.
Why Is This Duty Important to Project Su: This duty raises the whole team's ceiling. By helping people collaborate, take risks, and keep improving, it turns a group of individuals into a real agile team, which is what makes everything else on a project work better.
You might enjoy this duty if you care about people's growth, like facilitating more than directing, and find satisfaction in watching a team come into its own.
Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Agile Coach, with guides on agile, Scrum, and Kanban: https://www.atlassian.com/agile

Duty Description: The QA Analysis duty makes sure the product actually works before it reaches users. QA analysts write test plans and cases, put the product through its paces, and catch bugs and broken flows while they are still cheap to fix. In agile work they test continuously, checking each piece as it is built rather than waiting until the very end.
What Does It Take for This Duty To Succe: It takes sharp attention to detail, logical thinking, and the discipline to test methodically, plus skills like writing BDD scenarios and QA test plans. The best analysts stay curious about how something might break and communicate the issues they find clearly.
Why Is This Duty Important to Project Su: This duty protects quality and trust. Shipping something broken costs far more than catching it early, so by finding problems before launch, QA keeps the product reliable and the team's reputation intact.
You might enjoy this duty if you like finding the flaw everyone else missed, enjoy methodical work, and take pride in making sure things really work.
Where Can I Learn More?: MDN Web Docs, a trusted resource for building software: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Learn

Duty Description: The Graphic Design duty creates the visual pieces that give a product its personality, logos, icons, illustrations, and brand assets. Designers turn ideas into clean, recognizable visuals that help a product look polished and feel like itself. It is craft-focused work where small details add up to a strong overall impression.
What Does It Take for This Duty To Succe: It takes visual craft, an eye for hierarchy and detail, and skills like icon design and illustration. Add collaboration and openness to feedback, since visuals usually go through several rounds before they feel right.
Why Is This Duty Important to Project Su: This duty shapes how a product looks and feels at first glance. Strong visuals build trust and make a product memorable, tying the whole experience together so it feels professional and complete.
You might enjoy this duty if you love visual craft, enjoy making things look clean and clear, and get satisfaction from polishing details until they feel right.
Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

Duty Description: The UX Strategy duty connects the day-to-day design work to the bigger picture of the user experience. Strategists map user journeys, storyboard experiences, and shape how the whole product should feel over time, so individual screens add up to a coherent journey. It is high-level thinking that keeps design pointed at real user and business goals.
What Does It Take for This Duty To Succe: It takes strong strategic and systems thinking, an understanding of the full customer experience, and the ability to zoom out from single screens to the whole journey. Add advocacy and business sense to connect user needs with what the organization is trying to achieve.
Why Is This Duty Important to Project Su: This duty keeps design decisions aligned with a bigger goal instead of happening piece by piece. By mapping the journey and setting experience strategy, it makes sure the many parts of a product add up to something that genuinely works for users.
You might enjoy this duty if you like seeing the big picture, enjoy connecting the dots between user needs and business goals, and prefer shaping direction over polishing details.
Where Can I Learn More?: Nielsen Norman Group, a trusted source for UX research and design: https://www.nngroup.com/

Duty Description: The Product Operations duty sets up how a team actually works together. Ops people define working agreements, map team processes, choose the right agile method, and clarify who owns what, so the team runs smoothly instead of tripping over itself. It is the behind-the-scenes work that makes good collaboration possible.
What Does It Take for This Duty To Succe: It takes process thinking, facilitation, and a good feel for team dynamics, plus skills like agile method selection and defining working agreements. The best ops people balance structure with flexibility, since a process should help a team, not box it in.
Why Is This Duty Important to Project Su: This duty is what lets a team scale and stay healthy. By defining clear processes and agreements, it reduces confusion and conflict, freeing everyone else to focus on the actual work rather than on how to work together.
You might enjoy this duty if you like building systems that help people work better, enjoy smoothing out friction, and get satisfaction from a team that runs well.
Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Team Playbook, practical plays for healthy teamwork: https://www.atlassian.com/team-playbook

Duty Description: The Account Management duty owns the relationship with the client. Account managers keep communication clear, set expectations, and make sure the client feels heard while the team focuses on the work. Much of the job is trust-building, being the steady point of contact who keeps everyone aligned.
What Does It Take for This Duty To Succe: It takes strong relationship-building, communication, and business sense, plus the diplomacy to balance client wishes with what the team can deliver. Skills like stakeholder management and clear expectation-setting sit at the center of the role.
Why Is This Duty Important to Project Su: This duty keeps the client relationship healthy, which protects the whole project. By managing expectations and communication, it prevents misunderstandings that could derail the work and builds the kind of trust that leads to lasting partnerships.
You might enjoy this duty if you like working with people, enjoy being the trusted point of contact, and are good at balancing what a client wants with what is realistic.
Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Team Playbook, practical plays for healthy teamwork: https://www.atlassian.com/team-playbook

Duty Description: The Everyone duty covers the work that is not owned by one role but shared by the whole team. Things like giving sprint demos and writing AI prompts are part of everyone's job, whatever their specialty. It is a reminder that on an agile team, some responsibilities belong to all of us.
What Does It Take for This Duty To Succe: It takes the shared basics of good teamwork: clear communication, presentation skills, and a willingness to pitch in beyond your own lane. Comfort with common tools and a habit of helping wherever needed go a long way.
Why Is This Duty Important to Project Su: This duty reflects how real agile teams work, with people stepping up for shared tasks rather than staying strictly in their roles. That shared ownership is part of what makes a team resilient and keeps work from falling through the cracks.
You might enjoy contributing here if you like pitching in wherever you are needed, enjoy presenting the team's work, and believe the best teams share the load.
Where Can I Learn More?: Atlassian Team Playbook, practical plays for healthy teamwork: https://www.atlassian.com/team-playbook
